query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings, progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is governed by dislocation transmission behavior at the heterointerfaces. The severe lattice distortion and chemical short‐range order in high‐entropy alloys produces interfaces that under standard processing are only semi‐coherent and allow early dislocation crossing and localized plasticity. By engineering more coherent, chemically uniform interfaces (via modified deposition parameters or a thin interlayer), the barrier to dislocation transmission is increased, which delays creep deformation and yields a more uniformly progressing plasticity under sustained loads.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating consisting of alternating FCC and BCC high‐entropy alloy layers fabricated by physical vapor deposition under standard conditions, resulting in interfaces that are semi‐coherent and exhibit pronounced lattice distortions and chemical short‐range order.
generation.intervention: Modify the deposition process (for example, by adjusting substrate temperature, deposition rate, or introducing a thin interlayer of a minor element) to enhance the coherency and chemical uniformity of the FCC/BCC interfaces.
generation.conditions: Creep testing under sustained loading at an elevated temperature (but below the threshold for significant interdiffusion) over timescales of hours to days in an inert or ambient atmosphere where the multilayer architecture is retained.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfacial coherency and local lattice matching (or controlled misfit strain) at the FCC/BCC boundaries, which is influenced by chemically induced short-range order and severe lattice distortion.
generation.mechanism: Improved interface coherency raises the dislocation transmission barrier at the interfaces. In the baseline state the semi-coherent interfaces allow early dislocation transmission and local strain concentration that precipitate progressive creep deformation. By increasing interface coherency, dislocation pile-up is promoted and transmission is delayed, leading to a more distributed, uniform plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Multilayers with engineered coherent interfaces will exhibit a lower steady-state creep rate, higher apparent strength under sustained load, and a more uniform distribution of plastic deformation compared to the baseline coating with semi-coherent interfaces.
generation.baseline: Standard FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers produced under typical deposition conditions with semi-coherent interfaces that allow relatively facile dislocation transmission under sustained loading.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies as long as the multilayer structure is maintained at the nanoscale (i.e., individual layer thickness remains in the tens-of-nm range) and testing temperatures are below the onset of interdiffusion or phase transformation that would otherwise alter the designed heterointerfaces.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative impact of interface coherency on dislocation transmission and its translation into creep behavior is not well established for high-entropy-alloy systems, and the optimal processing window for achieving the desired interface structure remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multilayer coatings: one using standard deposition conditions (baseline) and one with modified deposition parameters or an engineered interlayer to promote enhanced interface coherency. Conduct constant-load creep experiments at an elevated temperature (below the diffusion threshold) for a fixed duration, while monitoring strain evolution over time. Supplement the mechanical testing with detailed TEM characterization of the interface structure.
measurements: TEM imaging to assess interfacial coherency and chemical uniformity
Creep strain rate measurements using high-resolution extensometry over the test duration
Post-test microstructural analysis (e.g., EBSD) to assess the distribution of deformation features
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayers engineered for higher interface coherency do not show a significantly reduced steady-state creep rate and a more uniform progression of plastic deformation compared to the baseline multilayers, the hypothesis will be rejected.
